result:
**About 1,600. The data gives no reason to think any two of the customer records are the same person.** 1,496 is the lowest the count could be, and you only get there by treating email as the only thing that identifies a person.

The counts come from `sahil-devx.dev_dna_silver.customers_master`:

| Measure | Count |
|---|---|
| Records (all current, none deleted) | 1,600 |
| Distinct customer IDs | 1,600 |
| Distinct phone numbers | 1,600 |
| Distinct names | 1,575 |
| Distinct emails | 1,496 |

**Why the lower counts don't mean duplicate people:**
- **Shared emails (103 emails used by 207 records, up to 3 each):** in none of these groups do the records share a name or a phone number. City, state, sign-up channel and sign-up date also differ. For example, `aaronconner@example.com` belongs to both Daniel Hall in Ahmedabad and Sandra Rivera in Jaipur. These look like reused or fake addresses, not one person with several records.
- **Shared names (26 pairs):** none share a phone or email, and only one pair shares a city. They're different people with the same name.

**Watch out for `dim_customer`.** Its description says it mirrors the customer master, but it has 1,496 rows, one per distinct email. It leaves out 104 customer IDs, so any report that joins to `dim_customer` will drop those customers' orders without any error.

If you have a different rule for deciding two records are the same person, such as email plus name, I can re-run the count with it. I also saved these findings to ktx memory so they come up in future questions.
